details.content: Principal Component Analysis is a dimensionality reduction technique that finds orthogonal directions, called principal components, which maximize the variance of the data.

Principal Component Analysis solution involves computing the data covariance matrix, performing eigenvalue decomposition of that matrix, and selecting the top M eigenvectors corresponding to the largest eigenvalues to form a new lower‑dimensional space.
The Lagrange function used to obtain the first principal component is L(u) = uᵀ C u - λ (uᵀ u - 1), where C is the covariance matrix and u is a unit vector.
Retaining too many principal components relative to the number of training samples can lead to overfitting.
A covariance matrix is a square, symmetric matrix that contains the covariances between each pair of dimensions in the original data space.
C = (1/N) Σ_{i=1}^{N} (x_i - μ)(x_i - μ)ᵀ, where μ is the mean vector of the data.
The covariance matrix is used in Principal Component Analysis to determine the directions of maximum variance.
An eigenvalue λ is a scalar that satisfies the equation A v = λ v for a given square matrix A and its corresponding eigenvector v.
det(A - λ I) = 0 defines the eigenvalues of matrix A.
An eigenvector v is a non‑zero vector that satisfies the equation A v = λ v for a given square matrix A and its corresponding eigenvalue λ.
Feature selection is the process of selecting a subset of relevant features for building a machine‑learning model, aiming to improve performance and reduce dimensionality.
High dimensionality of text features and the existence of irrelevant or noisy features can degrade model performance in text classification.
Feature selection techniques such as stop‑word removal, stemming, and discriminative word selection are employed to mitigate the problems of high dimensionality and noisy features.
Text classification is the task of assigning predefined categories to textual documents based on their content.
Effective feature selection is crucial for text classification because textual data often have very high dimensionality.
Bag of words is a document representation that treats a text as an unordered collection of word occurrences, ignoring grammar and word order.
Stop-word removal is a preprocessing step that eliminates common words such as articles, conjunctions, and prepositions from text to reduce noise.
Stemming reduces different morphological forms of a word—such as singular, plural, and various tenses—to a single base form.
Discriminative power of a word w measures how well the presence of w predicts the document's class, quantified by p_n(w) = Prob(document ∈ class n | it contains w).
The raw probability p_n(w) may be biased when the global class distribution of documents is not uniform.
A normalized probability q_n(w) = p_n(w) / P_n, where P_n is the fraction of documents belonging to class n, is used to compute a bias‑adjusted Gini index for word w.
The Gini index of a word w is defined as G(w) = Σ_{n=1}^{k} p_n(w)^2 and measures the impurity of w with respect to class distribution; higher values indicate stronger discriminative power.
A normalized Gini index using q_n(w) instead of p_n(w) mitigates bias caused by imbalanced class distributions.
